# Writing fast BPL

Write hot numerical code for static kinds, give data suitable widths, and express branches and updates with array operations. Whole-array expressions, trains and dfns use the same graph. Choose the spelling that reads best.

This guide describes the new core under construction. Its execution and cost claims are design targets, not measured performance promises for the released implementation. [Computational foundations](foundations.qmd) explains the design.

## Static kinds and widths

Put the setting at the start of a file or notebook cell. Choose widths for data and constants that the calculation will keep:

```bpl
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
x←[1 2 3]ₛ
i←[0 1 2]ₓ₄
rate←0.01ₛ
```

`ₛ` and `ₚ` select 32-bit and 64-bit floats. `ₓ₄` and `ₓ₈` select signed 32-bit and 64-bit integers. Fixed integers wrap on overflow. Choose a width that holds every intermediate you need, not only the inputs. Ordinary exact `ₓ` is not an explicit storage width.

Convert imported data once, or give its columns types when reading it. Keep loop state and branch results at compatible kinds and widths. A strong 64-bit float beside 32-bit data widens the arithmetic. A weak literal takes its partner's width. [Numbers](numbers.qmd) gives the promotion rules.

A wider reduction seed widens its accumulator without widening the stored input:

```bpl
0ₓ₈+/i
```

A result conversion such as `(+/)ₓ₈` happens after the reduction and cannot recover an overflow.

## Choose the intended numerical operation

Use the real forms `√ₐ`, `*ₐ`, `⍟ₐ` and `○ₐ` where values can leave a real domain and you want real results. These forms, including inverse-circle real forms, have value-independent result kinds and are required fast paths. Unmarked `√`, `*`, `⍟` and `○` have no such speed guarantee. The real forms preserve the arguments' promoted float width.

`fₐ` gives the real part of the principal result outside the real domain. For example, `√ₐ¯4` gives 0, not NaN or an error. Choose that meaning intentionally. Use Agenda when different inputs need different calculations.

`a÷ₓb` floors the quotient to an exact integer. It is the fast form for floor division, not exact rational division and not truncation towards zero. For a floating quotient, convert integer data to the intended float width before dividing. Use ordinary `÷` on exact integers when you need its numerical meaning, rather than replacing it for speed.

16-bit and complex operations use whole-array kernels, but this core does not fuse their steps into compiled block stages. Narrower storage alone does not guarantee faster execution.

Fusion and reassociation can change last bits, infinities and NaNs, and the sign of zero. They still follow the finite-result accuracy bounds and exact results on [Numbers](numbers.qmd#accuracy). The [target's approved numerical direction](target.qmd#numerical-algorithms) has not established new measured bounds.

## Work on arrays; write readable functions

These spellings express the same sum of squares:

```bpl
loss←+/⊼
loss x
{+/⊼⍵}x
```

Calling a dfn does not impose a different numerical execution route. Each, Rank and stencils can batch a function over its cells instead of calling an interpreter for every item. Prefer those operations to a user-written item loop. [Maps](evaluation.qmd#functions-and-effects) explains their cell model.

Use [index notation](index-notation.qmd) when naming the axes makes a formula easier to express. Named selections and contractions participate in the same read-mapping and product rules as whole-array spellings. Index notation is an option, not a requirement for speed.

Spaces are semantic. `+/÷≢ x` applies the mean train; `+/÷≢x` means something else. Use `⁝` to keep an operator's operand distinct from its argument without ending the run. Keep parentheses that clarify a compound operand. Follow [Composition](composition.qmd) and [Style](style.qmd), rather than removing punctuation to make code look faster.

## Select cases and update selected data

[Agenda](glyphs/diamond-underbar.qmd) chooses a calculation for each cell:

```bpl
(0≤)⍚[0 √ₐ] x
```

This gives zero for negative items and their square roots otherwise. Use Agenda instead of dfn guards on traced values in hot code. Static elementwise cases can use masked execution. Cases needing cross-item work, differing layouts or effects gather their selected cells first. Checked dynamic cases that can raise a data error gather their live cells from the outset.

[Under](glyphs/at.qmd) applies a function to a selection and writes its results back. `f@g` uses the selection that `g` makes. `f@[p]` uses the cells that predicate `p` picks. For example, `0@[0>]x` replaces negative items with zero.

Preallocate a cache and update its selected rows instead of rebuilding it at every step. Here `p` is the row position and `x+.×Wk` gives a row of 64 items:

```bpl
K←[1000 64]⍴0ₛ
K.[p]←x+.×Wk
```

Keep the update's kind compatible with the cache. Storage can be reused when no other value needs the old array. An alias or an observation of the old value can require a copy. [Assignment](assignment.ipynb) covers writes and value semantics.

Under static graph-numeric execution, invalid numeric indexed reads give the fill and invalid numeric writes skip those positions. Dynamic execution checks them. Shape, kind, name and host errors remain checked in both modes. Keep cache positions within their intended bounds.

## Keep repeated work inside a loop

[Power](glyphs/star-diaeresis.qmd) expresses a repeated step as one loop with a recorded body:

```bpl
n←100ₓ₄ ⋄ step⍣n⁝params
```

Here `step` is the update function and `params` its initial state. A Python loop that repeatedly calls BPL rebuilds each call's graph. Keeping iteration in BPL avoids that construction work. A loop's derivative and batching rules transform its body through the same execution system.

Stable kinds and shapes across calls and iterations make reuse easier. A changed length does not automatically compile another version. The length key distinguishes 0, 1 and more; within a class, refill updates concrete shapes and read mappings while the plan's other assumptions hold. Changed kinds, ranks, structural parameters, axis equalities or range assumptions can require another plan. The JIT compiles worthwhile structural versions on demand, with counts passed at runtime.

A growing state needs more allocation and copying than a fixed-capacity cache. Preallocation is often clearer and cheaper even when refill permits plan reuse.

## Understand reads and recording stops

An assignment or local name does not force a numerical result. A read computes the pending work it reaches. Display, conversion to Python, a guard reading an item value, structural parameters, data-dependent counts and operand reads required by a call are read boundaries. A data-dependent length can continue through count read and refill without ending the recording. Output and other effects force only their own operands and keep their order.

Recording stops at host control flow depending on traced values, calls with host-kind data, recursion, `⍎`, error guards, writes to outer bindings and effects that change bindings or settings. A stopped recording runs ordinary code. Under `∂`, writing a differentiated value to an outer binding is an error. A dfn guard on a framed value can become a select, but guards on traced values are not fast-code targets. [Automatic differentiation](autodiff.qmd) covers differentiation-specific boundaries.

Dynamic kinds remain intended for interactive analysis. The design target is correct execution within four times the equivalent static-kind code at the same size, except agreed cases. An ordinary run builds nodes and looks up plans. A cache miss also schedules the graph. Recorded bodies reuse that construction and scheduling. Neither static kinds nor the JIT makes every small call free.

## Inspect the work

Use [`•explain`](system/explain.qmd) on a representative expression. Inspect `stopped` and `fallbacks` for host execution, `forced` for intermediate reads, `stored` for materialized intermediates, and `programs` and `compiles` for reuse. A stored value is sometimes the right schedule; investigate its reason instead of trying to eliminate every record.

[`•memory`](system/memory.qmd) reports retained values and bytes. [`•storage`](system/storage.qmd) shows how an array is held. When several Python worker processes compete for cores, [`•prefs`](system/prefs.qmd) with `"threads":1` keeps each on one thread. The browser runs block stages without the native JIT.
